en: Viscous lava cools quickly and solidifies near the vent, repeatedly stacking to build Mayon Volcano's famously steep and perfect conical shape.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the underground limestone rock, carving out the massive cave system of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River.
Tiny coral polyps extract calcium from seawater to build hard skeletons, which accumulate over centuries to form the Tubbataha Reefs.
Moisture-heavy Habagat winds blow from the ocean, hit the Zambales Mountains, and are forced upward to release heavy rainfall over western Luzon.
Magma heats underground water into high-pressure steam at Mount Makiling, which then rises to spin turbines and generate geothermal electricity.
Ancient stone walls on the Banaue Rice Terraces slow down water runoff, trapping soil and preventing erosion on steep mountain slopes.
Massive volcanic eruptions emptied shallow magma chambers, causing the ground to collapse into a large caldera that eventually filled with rainwater to form Lake Taal.
Rising sea levels after the last ice age submerged land bridges, isolating Palawan's mainland animals and causing them to evolve into unique species.
The Philippine Sea Plate slides beneath the Eurasian Plate at the Philippine Trench, and the friction releases built-up stress as powerful earthquakes.
Ocean waves continuously crush dead coral and shells into tiny calcium carbonate fragments, washing them ashore to create Boracay's famous white sand beaches.
The Cagayan River slows down as it reaches the Babuyan Channel, dropping its carried sediment to build a wide, fertile river delta.
Underwater volcanic eruptions continuously push fresh lava and ash upward through Lake Taal, gradually building the landmass of Volcano Island.
